name: settings-cmd-comma
description:
Cmd+comma opens the settings window, and the /settings route inside it loads.

The chord is claimed in prePerformKeyEquivalent, on the raw NSEvent, not through the IDC seam. Measured: on an HTML surface this chord reaches prePerform and never postPerform, so the intercept decision never sees it and un-gating that alone brings nothing back.

This also proves a requirement that a restored tab could not: a top-chrome URL will not load as an ordinary tab (measured, ERR_INVALID_URL). It needs a host, and this is the host.

Every assertion here was measured on the run BEFORE the chord was sent - the window count was 1, and neither settings line was in the log.

The rail is a 190px left column, so a click at fixed coordinates lands on whatever sits there. This selects each pane by '.settings-rail-item[data-pane]'.click() and read the '.selected' class back, the same element-targeted pattern the-native-view-toggle-fades-in.json and the-appearance-pane-picks-the-app-icon.json already use.

actions.note: gate: the startup tab committed, so the app is up
Atrium frontmost, so the chord reaches it
let the window build and its route load
evidence of the settings window and its pane rail

actions.expression: (() => { const b = document.querySelector('.settings-rail-item[data-pane="appearance"]'); if (!b) return 'no-pane'; b.click(); return document.querySelector('.settings-rail-item[data-pane="appearance"].selected') ? 'selected' : 'not-selected'; })()
actions.note: the Appearance pane in the rail. The rail is a 190px LEFT column, so a fixed coordinate lands on blank space. Selecting by '.settings-rail-item[data-pane]' and reading the '.selected' class back is the pattern the-native-view-toggle-fades-in.json and the-appearance-pane-picks-the-app-icon.json already use for this exact rail.
evidence of the Appearance rows and their values

actions.expression: (() => { const b = document.querySelector('.settings-rail-item[data-pane="inputs"]'); if (!b) return 'no-pane'; b.click(); return document.querySelector('.settings-rail-item[data-pane="inputs"].selected') ? 'selected' : 'not-selected'; })()
actions.note: the Inputs pane in the rail - same element-click pattern as select-appearance above, not a fixed coordinate
evidence of the shortcut rows built from the hotkeys store

actions.expression: (() => { const b = document.querySelector('.settings-rail-item[data-pane="spaces"]'); if (!b) return 'no-pane'; b.click(); return document.querySelector('.settings-rail-item[data-pane="spaces"].selected') ? 'selected' : 'not-selected'; })()
actions.note: the Spaces pane in the rail - same element-click pattern, not a fixed coordinate
evidence of the space list and the detail panel

assertions.label: the-chord-reached-the-menu-item
assertions.note: There is no prePerform claim to match. The chord completes the renderer round trip, reaches postPerform, and fires the retargeted Settings item - so this line is what says the chord arrived

assertions.label: the-route-loaded-and-answered
assertions.note: settingsReady only arrives when the /settings module ran and chrome.send reached the host. This is what a tab could not prove
the browser window AND the settings window. One means the chord did nothing

assertions.label: the-core-supplied-the-values
assertions.note: the General rows read from the Rust core. This line only appears after settingsReady, and only when atrium_core_query answered - it is the read path that did not exist at all after the Swift cut

assertions.label: the-core-supplied-the-hotkeys
assertions.note: the Inputs pane's shortcut rows come from the hotkeys store, read through the core the same way settings are

assertions.label: the-core-supplied-the-spaces
assertions.note: the Spaces pane edits spaces, so it takes the whole document rather than one window's sidebar model
